summary: Sirach 42 first tells readers not to be ashamed of justice, honest accounting, correction, and careful record keeping. It then gives anxious household counsel about daughters and women in an ancient patriarchal setting. The chapter turns sharply into praise of the Lord’s works, wisdom, knowledge, and glory displayed through all things.
whyItMatters: This chapter shows Sirach’s range: practical instruction about ordinary social life stands beside a hymn-like reflection on creation and divine knowledge. It also contains counsel about women and household power that needs careful historical distance rather than easy modern application.

context.author: Yeshua (Jesus) son of Eleazar son of Sira, a Jerusalem teacher and scribe; the Greek translation was made later by his unnamed grandson.
context.audience: Students seeking disciplined wisdom in Jerusalem, and later Greek-reading Jews in Egypt or the wider diaspora.
context.date: The Hebrew work was composed in the early second century BC and was likely complete around 180–175 BC. The grandson arrived in Egypt around 132 BC and translated it during his stay.
context.setting: Jerusalem under Hellenistic rule, with Torah study, temple worship, household authority, trade, and Greek-speaking Mediterranean culture in view.
context.literaryForm: Wisdom instruction using maxims, warnings, paired lines, catalogues, and hymn-like praise.

outline.heading: Do not be ashamed of upright conduct
outline.note: The teacher lists situations where shame should not keep someone from justice, careful accounting, correction, and written records.

outline.heading: Anxious counsel about daughters
outline.note: A father’s concern is described through fears about a daughter’s sexuality, marriage, public reputation, and family shame.

outline.heading: Warnings about women
outline.note: The chapter gives severe, patriarchal warnings about women and shame; readers should notice the ancient household setting and the unequal assumptions.

outline.heading: The Lord’s works and glory
outline.note: The speaker turns from household instruction to declaring the works of the Lord, whose works are full of glory and exceed human power to declare fully.

outline.heading: The Most High knows hidden things
outline.note: God searches the deep and the heart, knows past and future, and needs no counselor.

outline.heading: The ordered beauty of all things
outline.note: The chapter closes by admiring all the works of God, their order, their pairs and opposites, and the inexhaustible sight of his glory.

keyVerses.text: Don’t be ashamed of these things, and don’t sin to save face:
keyVerses.why: This opening line frames the first movement: shame must not push a person away from right conduct.

keyVerses.text: Whatever you hand over, let it be by number and weight. In giving and receiving, let all be in writing.
keyVerses.why: This verse captures the chapter’s practical wisdom about accountability in ordinary exchanges.

keyVerses.text: He searches out the deep and the heart. He has understanding of their secrets. For the Most High knows all knowledge. He sees the signs of the world.
keyVerses.why: The verse anchors the chapter’s second half, where divine knowledge reaches what humans cannot see.

keyVerses.text: One thing establishes the good things of another. Who could ever see enough of his glory?
keyVerses.why: The final question leaves the reader with wonder rather than a closed explanation of creation.

questions.question: Why does the chapter begin by saying not to be ashamed?
questions.answer: The opening section names situations where a person might feel social pressure: applying the law, doing justice, reckoning with partners, handling goods, bargaining, correcting children, and instructing the foolish. The point is not that every action listed is comfortable to modern readers, but that shame should not prevent integrity in public and household life.

questions.question: What does “save face” mean here?
questions.answer: In this verse, “save face” means protecting public appearance or reputation. The teacher warns that avoiding embarrassment can become a reason to sin. The phrase sets up the chapter’s concern with honor, shame, and public approval.

questions.question: Why does Sirach care so much about weights, counting, and writing things down?
questions.answer: Verses 3-7 picture ordinary transactions with partners, travellers, friends, merchants, and property. The advice favors exactness, numbering, weighing, locking things up, and written records. The chapter treats careful documentation as part of wise conduct, not as distrust by itself.

questions.question: How should a first-time reader handle the line about making “the back of an evil slave to bleed”?
questions.answer: The verse assumes an ancient household world that included slavery and corporal punishment. The chapter states the counsel without challenging that institution. Historical context helps explain the social world of the text, but it should not be turned into permission to harm vulnerable people.

questions.question: Why is the section about daughters so anxious?
questions.answer: Verses 9–11 describe a father losing sleep over a daughter’s youth, virginity, marriage, possible pregnancy, barrenness, reputation, and public shame. The worries are framed from the father’s point of view inside a patriarchal household. His concern is family honor and control of a daughter’s sexuality; her own perspective is absent from the counsel.

questions.question: Are verses 12-14 saying women are worse than men?
questions.answer: The wording is harsh and reflects suspicion of women within an ancient male teaching context. Verse 14 even says, “Better is the wickedness of a man than a pleasant woman,” which is not a neutral statement about men and women. Responsible reading should name the patriarchal double standard rather than smoothing it over.

questions.question: Why does the chapter shift from household warnings to the works of the Lord?
questions.answer: Sirach often moves between ordinary conduct and praise of God, because wisdom is meant to include both daily behavior and reflection on creation. Here the turn begins in verse 15: “I will make mention now of the works of the Lord.” The chapter’s second half expands the reader’s view from human shame and household order to divine wisdom and glory.

questions.question: What does the chapter say God knows?
questions.answer: It says God searches “the deep and the heart,” understands secrets, knows all knowledge, sees signs, declares past and future things, and reveals hidden traces. The language does not explain how this knowledge works. It presents divine knowledge as complete where human declaration is limited.

questions.question: What does “all things are in pairs” mean in the closing lines?
questions.answer: Verse 24 says, “All things are in pairs, one opposite the other,” and connects this with God making nothing imperfect. The chapter points to an ordered creation in which things answer, contrast, or complete one another. It does not give a scientific system; it is a wisdom reflection on order, usefulness, and glory.

glossary.def: A title for God used in the chapter when speaking of God’s law and complete knowledge.
A binding relationship or obligation; in this chapter it appears with the law of the Most High.
Tools for measuring goods fairly in trade or exchange.
A public label or saying attached to someone’s disgrace.
The things God has made or done, especially the ordered creation praised in the second half of the chapter.
The visible weight, honor, or splendor associated here with the Lord’s work and ordered creation.
